items.title: How Aiden Agents Survive Running Out of Context Mid-Task: A Technical Deep Dive
items.summary: Every long-running AI agent eventually hits the same wall: the active context window can no longer hold everything the task needs, either because the conversation itself has grown too large, or because a single tool call has returned more data than fits in what’s left of the budget. This is not an edge case. It is a structural certainty for any agent architecture that runs multi-step tasks over a bounded context window, and how a system responds to it says more about its production-readiness than almost any other design decision. This week we shipped real infrastructure for this in Aiden’s firmware, across three merged pull requests: #497 , #498 , and #530 . This piece is a deep look at the mechanism, the design reasoning behind it, and its explicit limits. The failure mode, precisely defined A context window has to simultaneously hold relevant instructions, recent conversation history, tool outputs, prior observations, and enough headroom for the model to generate its next response. Two distinct conditions can exceed that budget: Cumulative overflow. A task runs long enough, across enough turns, that accumulated history exceeds the provider’s context limit even though no single message was large. Single-event overflow. One tool call returns a result too large to fit in the remaining budget regardless of how much history preceded it — a research tool returning extensive source material, a file-processing tool returning a large directory listing or log, or a desktop-automation loop accumulating detailed interface observations across many screens. Both conditions produce the same practical failure if left unhandled. And critically, there are exactly two naive responses to this failure, and both are unacceptable in a production agent: Hard failure. The task simply stops. No path to resume, no partial credit for work already completed. Blind restart. The agent starts over with incomplete or reconstructed history and, lacking a reliable record of what it already did, silently repeats work — re-collecting sources already reviewed, reprocessing files already handled, or worse, reattempting a device action that may have already succeeded. That second failure mode deserves particular scrutiny for a system like Aiden, which is designed for user-directed interaction with real smartphone and computer interfaces. A context-window error is a property of the model request. It says nothing about whether the external device state changed. An agent that treats “I lost my context” as equivalent to “nothing happened yet” is making an unjustified inference, and for a physical agent capable of tapping buttons and submitting forms, that’s not a cosmetic bug. Architecture: what actually shipped The implementation spans a genuinely cross-cutting set of concerns: Go for the agent runtime, HTTP and LLM provider API integration, message serialization, file-based persistence, and a Python evaluation framework for testing recovery behavior. That breadth matters, because a reliable recovery path is not solvable purely at the prompt layer — it requires provider-facing limit handling, durable task-artifact storage, and a way to empirically test whether resumed behavior is actually justified. The system implements three coordinated behaviors: Context compression. When the active context cannot continue as-is, the runtime reduces it to a smaller, decision-relevant representation. This is explicitly lossy — compression can and does omit detail — which is why compression alone is never treated as sufficient grounds to continue. Session switching. The task can move to a refreshed interaction or session when the previous one has reached its usable limit. Critically, a new session is not treated as a blank slate; it still requires the preserved task information described below to be useful rather than just another restart in disguise. Saved-result-file recovery. This is the core of the design. Rather than relying solely on in-context summarization to preserve continuity, the system persists task-relevant state to a file outside the active context window entirely, and reads it back deliberately at the moment of recovery. The recovery read: four specific pieces of evidence This is the architecturally interesting part, and it’s worth being precise about exactly what gets read, because the design principle is recovery-as-decision, not recovery-as-default. Before deciding whether to continue, the system reads: Continuation ID — connects the recovery attempt to the specific prior execution or continuation chain it belongs to. Without this, a recovered state has no reliable anchor to the task it’s supposed to be resuming. Saved state — recorded information about progress: what’s completed, what’s pending, what phase the task is in. Saved errors — this is what allows the system to distinguish a benign context-limit event from a different, potentially more serious failure that should not be silently continued through. A context overflow and a tool failure look similar from the outside if you don’t preserve the distinction explicitly. Previous output tail — the most recent portion of prior output, useful for recovering the immediate “what was I doing” context, but explicitly not a complete execution history. It’s a clue, not a ledger. The system then evaluates whether this evidence is sufficient to justify continuing, retrying with additional verification, or stopping and surfacing the situation for human review. That three-way branch — continue / verify-then-retry / stop-and-surface — is the actual design contribution here. A simpler implementation would collapse this to a binary continue-or-fail; treating “uncertain” as its own first-class outcome, distinct from both success and hard failure, is what makes this a recovery decision rather than an automatic default. There’s a design question underneath this worth making explicit: why persist to a file at all, rather than just summarizing more aggressively within the context window itself? The answer is a separation-of-concerns argument. Task bookkeeping — what step you’re on, what a prior tool call returned, whether anything errored — is not reasoning content. It doesn’t need to survive inside the same budget-constrained space the model uses to think. Conflating the two means a context-overflow event destroys both simultaneously: the model’s working reasoning and the durable facts about what actually happened. Externalizing the latter to a recoverable file means an overflow event only costs you the former. This is not a novel insight in isolated terms — durable-execution patterns in agent orchestration frameworks make a similar argument. LangGraph’s durable execution documentation describes checkpointing workflow state so that a process can resume from the last successful step rather than replaying from scratch, and explicitly separates this from in-context memory. Provider-level conversation state management follows a related but distinct pattern: OpenAI’s conversation-state documentation describes options ranging from resending full message history to using a persistent conversation object specifically to avoid re-deriving context on every request. Aiden’s saved-result-file approach sits closer to the checkpoint model than the conversation-object model, because the recovery artifact is designed to be read selectively (four specific fields) rather than replayed wholesale. Where this connects to Aiden’s broader reliability model Aiden’s real-device interaction loop follows an observe → interpret → act → verify pattern — a conceptual framework for how the agent should behave when acting on a visible interface, not a claim about a specific named internal architecture. Context recovery adds a continuity check to that loop: when the active session can’t continue, the agent inspects persisted execution evidence before choosing its next action, and for interface-facing tasks specifically, it should also re-observe the current interface state rather than trusting that a stale checkpoint still accurately describes it. This distinction — saved record versus fresh observation — matters more here than in a purely text-based agent. A saved record says what the agent believed happened. A fresh screen observation shows what the device currently displays. For a physical agent, both forms of evidence may be independently necessary; neither substitutes for the other. Explicit limits, stated without hedging This is not a universal recovery layer, and the failure modes below are not hypothetical edge cases — they’re the actual boundary of what this system does and doesn’t handle: Compression is lossy by construction. It can omit detail that later turns out to matter. Saved state can itself be missing, stale, partial, or corrupted. The recovery path has to handle the case where the recovery artifact itself isn’t trustworthy, not just the happy path where it is. This does not cover every interruption class. Provider outages, network failures, tool failures unrelated to size, authentication issues, and unexpected device/interface states can all still interrupt a task, and none of them are addressed by this specific mechanism. No exactly-once guarantee. This system reduces the likelihood of duplicate or lost work; it does not provide formal exactly-once execution semantics the way some distributed systems literature would require for that label. How this should actually be tested For anyone building something comparable, here’s the test matrix we consider necessary, not just sufficient, for validating a context-overflow recovery path: Test area What to validate Provider-limit recovery Continuation ID, state, errors, and output tail are all read before any continuation decision Oversized tool outputs Recovery doesn’t silently discard task-critical information during compression Malformed saved files The system fails safely — stop, report, or request review — when persisted data can’t be trusted Partial completion Behavior is correct when one step completed before the next triggered an interruption Duplicate-action risk The system can distinguish completed, partially-completed, and unstarted work wherever possible Session handoff A fresh session receives bounded, relevant continuation information rather than starting blind Changed device state Changing the visible interface between checkpoint and resume forces a fresh observation rather than trusting the stale checkpoint Human controls Pause, interruption, redirection, review, and confirmation paths all function correctly mid-recovery Notice that several of these tests are specifically designed to break naive implementations — malformed saved files and changed device state in particular are the tests most likely to expose a system that looks correct in the demo case but fails under real-world conditions. The honest summary This work turns one specific, common failure mode — running out of context mid-task — from “restart and hope nothing important got lost” into a deliberate recovery decision grounded in persisted evidence. It does not create unlimited context. It does not guarantee every interrupted task can finish safely. It does not replace testing, verification, or human oversight for consequential actions. What it does is make “continue” a decision the system can justify, rather than a default it falls into. Every long-running AI agent eventually hits the same wall: the active context window can no longer hold everything the task needs, either because the conversation itself has grown too large, or because a single tool call has returned more data than fits in what’s left of the budget. This is not an edge case. It is a structural certainty for any agent architecture that runs multi-step tasks over a bounded context window, and how a system responds to it says more about its production-readiness than almost any other design decision.

This week we shipped real infrastructure for this in Aiden’s firmware, across three merged pull requests: #497, #498, and #530. This piece is a deep look at the mechanism, the design reasoning behind it, and its explicit limits.

The failure mode, precisely defined

A context window has to simultaneously hold relevant instructions, recent conversation history, tool outputs, prior observations, and enough headroom for the model to generate its next response. Two distinct conditions can exceed that budget:

  1. Cumulative overflow. A task runs long enough, across enough turns, that accumulated history exceeds the provider’s context limit even though no single message was large.
  2. Single-event overflow. One tool call returns a result too large to fit in the remaining budget regardless of how much history preceded it — a research tool returning extensive source material, a file-processing tool returning a large directory listing or log, or a desktop-automation loop accumulating detailed interface observations across many screens.

Both conditions produce the same practical failure if left unhandled. And critically, there are exactly two naive responses to this failure, and both are unacceptable in a production agent:

  • Hard failure. The task simply stops. No path to resume, no partial credit for work already completed.
  • Blind restart. The agent starts over with incomplete or reconstructed history and, lacking a reliable record of what it already did, silently repeats work — re-collecting sources already reviewed, reprocessing files already handled, or worse, reattempting a device action that may have already succeeded.

That second failure mode deserves particular scrutiny for a system like Aiden, which is designed for user-directed interaction with real smartphone and computer interfaces. A context-window error is a property of the model request. It says nothing about whether the external device state changed. An agent that treats “I lost my context” as equivalent to “nothing happened yet” is making an unjustified inference, and for a physical agent capable of tapping buttons and submitting forms, that’s not a cosmetic bug.

Architecture: what actually shipped

The implementation spans a genuinely cross-cutting set of concerns: Go for the agent runtime, HTTP and LLM provider API integration, message serialization, file-based persistence, and a Python evaluation framework for testing recovery behavior. That breadth matters, because a reliable recovery path is not solvable purely at the prompt layer — it requires provider-facing limit handling, durable task-artifact storage, and a way to empirically test whether resumed behavior is actually justified.

The system implements three coordinated behaviors:

Context compression. When the active context cannot continue as-is, the runtime reduces it to a smaller, decision-relevant representation. This is explicitly lossy — compression can and does omit detail — which is why compression alone is never treated as sufficient grounds to continue.

Session switching. The task can move to a refreshed interaction or session when the previous one has reached its usable limit. Critically, a new session is not treated as a blank slate; it still requires the preserved task information described below to be useful rather than just another restart in disguise.

Saved-result-file recovery. This is the core of the design. Rather than relying solely on in-context summarization to preserve continuity, the system persists task-relevant state to a file outside the active context window entirely, and reads it back deliberately at the moment of recovery.

The recovery read: four specific pieces of evidence

This is the architecturally interesting part, and it’s worth being precise about exactly what gets read, because the design principle is recovery-as-decision, not recovery-as-default.

Before deciding whether to continue, the system reads:

  1. Continuation ID — connects the recovery attempt to the specific prior execution or continuation chain it belongs to. Without this, a recovered state has no reliable anchor to the task it’s supposed to be resuming.
  2. Saved state — recorded information about progress: what’s completed, what’s pending, what phase the task is in.
  3. Saved errors — this is what allows the system to distinguish a benign context-limit event from a different, potentially more serious failure that should not be silently continued through. A context overflow and a tool failure look similar from the outside if you don’t preserve the distinction explicitly.
  4. Previous output tail — the most recent portion of prior output, useful for recovering the immediate “what was I doing” context, but explicitly not a complete execution history. It’s a clue, not a ledger.

The system then evaluates whether this evidence is sufficient to justify continuing, retrying with additional verification, or stopping and surfacing the situation for human review. That three-way branch — continue / verify-then-retry / stop-and-surface — is the actual design contribution here. A simpler implementation would collapse this to a binary continue-or-fail; treating “uncertain” as its own first-class outcome, distinct from both success and hard failure, is what makes this a recovery decision rather than an automatic default.

There’s a design question underneath this worth making explicit: why persist to a file at all, rather than just summarizing more aggressively within the context window itself?

The answer is a separation-of-concerns argument. Task bookkeeping — what step you’re on, what a prior tool call returned, whether anything errored — is not reasoning content. It doesn’t need to survive inside the same budget-constrained space the model uses to think. Conflating the two means a context-overflow event destroys both simultaneously: the model’s working reasoning and the durable facts about what actually happened. Externalizing the latter to a recoverable file means an overflow event only costs you the former.

This is not a novel insight in isolated terms — durable-execution patterns in agent orchestration frameworks make a similar argument. LangGraph’s durable execution documentation describes checkpointing workflow state so that a process can resume from the last successful step rather than replaying from scratch, and explicitly separates this from in-context memory. Provider-level conversation state management follows a related but distinct pattern: OpenAI’s conversation-state documentation describes options ranging from resending full message history to using a persistent conversation object specifically to avoid re-deriving context on every request. Aiden’s saved-result-file approach sits closer to the checkpoint model than the conversation-object model, because the recovery artifact is designed to be read selectively (four specific fields) rather than replayed wholesale.

Where this connects to Aiden’s broader reliability model

Aiden’s real-device interaction loop follows an observe → interpret → act → verify pattern — a conceptual framework for how the agent should behave when acting on a visible interface, not a claim about a specific named internal architecture. Context recovery adds a continuity check to that loop: when the active session can’t continue, the agent inspects persisted execution evidence before choosing its next action, and for interface-facing tasks specifically, it should also re-observe the current interface state rather than trusting that a stale checkpoint still accurately describes it.

This distinction — saved record versus fresh observation — matters more here than in a purely text-based agent. A saved record says what the agent believed happened. A fresh screen observation shows what the device currently displays. For a physical agent, both forms of evidence may be independently necessary; neither substitutes for the other.

Explicit limits, stated without hedging

This is not a universal recovery layer, and the failure modes below are not hypothetical edge cases — they’re the actual boundary of what this system does and doesn’t handle:

  • Compression is lossy by construction. It can omit detail that later turns out to matter.
  • Saved state can itself be missing, stale, partial, or corrupted. The recovery path has to handle the case where the recovery artifact itself isn’t trustworthy, not just the happy path where it is.
  • This does not cover every interruption class. Provider outages, network failures, tool failures unrelated to size, authentication issues, and unexpected device/interface states can all still interrupt a task, and none of them are addressed by this specific mechanism.
  • No exactly-once guarantee. This system reduces the likelihood of duplicate or lost work; it does not provide formal exactly-once execution semantics the way some distributed systems literature would require for that label.

For anyone building something comparable, here’s the test matrix we consider necessary, not just sufficient, for validating a context-overflow recovery path:

The honest summary

This work turns one specific, common failure mode — running out of context mid-task — from “restart and hope nothing important got lost” into a deliberate recovery decision grounded in persisted evidence. It does not create unlimited context. It does not guarantee every interrupted task can finish safely. It does not replace testing, verification, or human oversight for consequential actions. What it does is make “continue” a decision the system can justify, rather than a default it falls into.

items.title: ChatGPT expands its foothold in the nation's classrooms
items.summary: ChatGPT for Teachers is expanding for the new school year. Philipp von Ditfurth/picture alliance via Getty Images OpenAI is roughly doubling the footprint of its ChatGPT for Teachers product. The tool is a free version of the company's business plan, part of a bid to woo educators. More than 2 million US students now live in districts signed up for the product, OpenAI says. Teachers are heading back to school, and ChatGPT is coming with them. OpenAI announced 55 new partnerships with American school districts on Wednesday, roughly doubling the reach of its ChatGPT for Teachers product. The districts signed on represent more than 300,000 staffers and 2 million students. The product, a slightly tweaked version of OpenAI's traditional business offering, aims to bring teachers on board with AI tools and give districts oversight. The product is strictly for adults, since OpenAI is not yet integrating student accounts or student-facing features. Not everyone is on board with AI in the classroom, as more students use it to complete assignments. A Pew Research Center survey last year found that more than half of teenagers have used AI chatbots for help with schoolwork, and more still believe their peers have used them to cheat. Some parents have begun organizing against AI in schools . Leah Belsky, OpenAI's vice president of education, said in a press briefing about the ChatGPT for Teachers rollout that improvements in AI's capabilities make "teacher judgment, teacher guidance, and district oversight even more important than before." OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teachers last November and has committed to keeping it free through June 2028. Districts in 30 states have now onboarded with the tool, OpenAI said, with the densest uptake in the Los Angeles area and in the Northeast. The company said several of the nation's largest school districts now participate, including Houston's. OpenAI's product includes onboarding and prompts tailored to educators. A company webpage suggests that teachers use ChatGPT to develop lesson plans and explanations on topics. OpenAI says it doesn't train its models for this product on information users submit to the chatbot. The company has also signed data privacy agreements that cover 16 states, it said. The company will provide its latest AI models to the product in "waves," Belsky said, adding, "The goal is really to keep teachers and districts at the frontier." She also said she hopes the product will help teachers "save time, support students, and strengthen their own professional judgment." Christine Mai, the Houston district's director of innovation, said on the briefing that her district has used ChatGPT to help staff write curricula and summarize documents. She said there has to be a "human in the loop." "The teacher is still the professional, right?" Mai said. "They still need to make the final judgment in terms of, if they're going to use AI in that way, then they are also responsible for making sure that it's accurate, that it actually will benefit the students." items.title: Xbox’s new disc-to-digital program gives physical games a digital future
items.summary: For decades, console owners have faced a choice between the convenience of digital downloads and the permanence of physical game discs. Soon, Xbox owners will be able to get the best of both worlds for thousands of supported titles as part of a newly announced disc-to-digital program. The program— announced today ahead of testing for Xbox Insiders starting August 31—will let players claim a "digital entitlement" for "most Xbox One and Xbox Series X disc-based games" simply by inserting the disc into a console and launching it. That game will then be playable completely digitally, without the need to ever insert the disc, as long as you (or a member of your family account) is logged in. The digital entitlement will also allow access to features like Xbox Play Anywhere (for play on PC) and Xbox Cloud Gaming, for supported titles. Microsoft says that your physical disc will "continue to work exactly as it always has" after the digital entitlement is claimed. But before you get any ideas, the fine print on the announcement mentions that there is only "one revokable license per game disc," so if you resell that disc or loan it to a friend, that digital entitlement could be transferred to a new account when someone else puts it into their console. For decades, console owners have faced a choice between the convenience of digital downloads and the permanence of physical game discs. Soon, Xbox owners will be able to get the best of both worlds for thousands of supported titles as part of a newly announced disc-to-digital program.

The program—announced today ahead of testing for Xbox Insiders starting August 31—will let players claim a "digital entitlement" for "most Xbox One and Xbox Series X disc-based games" simply by inserting the disc into a console and launching it. That game will then be playable completely digitally, without the need to ever insert the disc, as long as you (or a member of your family account) is logged in. The digital entitlement will also allow access to features like Xbox Play Anywhere (for play on PC) and Xbox Cloud Gaming, for supported titles.

Microsoft says that your physical disc will "continue to work exactly as it always has" after the digital entitlement is claimed. But before you get any ideas, the fine print on the announcement mentions that there is only "one revokable license per game disc," so if you resell that disc or loan it to a friend, that digital entitlement could be transferred to a new account when someone else puts it into their console.

items.title: Claude Desktop can now easily run Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi models — after Ollama’s first effort stalled
items.summary: Open-weight model runner Ollama has reintroduced an integration with Claude Desktop that lets users connect Anthropic’s app to models served through Ollama, including models running locally on their own machines. This effectively means Claude users can tap Ollama’s library, which includes popular models such as Qwen , DeepSeek , Kimi , and GLM , while remaining inside the Claude Desktop interface — with Ollama serving as the gateway to whichever model is handling the request. Ollama’s model catalog inside Claude Desktop A second shot at Claude Desktop This isn’t Ollama’s first attempt to bring its model catalog to Anthropic’s tools. Back in January, the company added support for Anthropic’s Messages API, allowing Claude Code to be pointed at Ollama and use local or cloud-hosted models instead of Claude. In April, Anthropic quietly opened a similar opportunity within the Claude Desktop app, adding a developer setting that let it connect to third-party inference gateways. Ollama seized on that with ollama launch claude-desktop , which configured the desktop app to use Ollama, however, the integration lasted mere days — following a Claude Desktop update, users found that the app’s gateway accepted the connection but rejected non-Anthropic model IDs. And so Ollama removed the feature , saying Claude Desktop’s third-party integration had become “limited to Anthropic models.” Fast forward to Aug. 21, and Ollama quietly introduced a new implementation in v0.33.0 that addresses that mismatch with a dedicated local proxy for Claude Desktop. In a blog post published on Tuesday formally announcing the support, Ollama notes that developers can now configure Claude Desktop to use it as a “third-party gateway provider.” The setup is handled from Ollama itself: users open the Ollama app, select Claude and switch the integration on, after which Ollama configures Claude Desktop’s third-party gateway automatically. Switching it off restores the user’s previous Claude setup. Enabling Claude Desktop As part of the update, Ollama has also put that Claude integration directly in its Mac menu, where users can toggle “Use Ollama models” on or off. Use Ollama models Once enabled, models available through Ollama — whether running locally or through Ollama Cloud — appear inside Claude Desktop’s own model picker, allowing users to select one without leaving Anthropic’s app. Claude Desktop model picker Because Claude Desktop is built around Anthropic’s own model options, Ollama also lets users decide which underlying model should sit behind each of those slots. In the example below, selecting “Opus 5” would route the request to Kimi K3, while “Sonnet 5” is mapped to DeepSeek V4 Pro. Auto Mode option It is also worth noting that the “Auto mode” option preserves Claude Desktop’s built-in Auto mode, which lets the app decide when it should ask the user for permission before making changes. Community questions The launch prompted a swathe of questions from the community on X, perhaps chief among them: why use an alternative model through Claude Desktop rather than simply use Claude? The answer, perhaps somewhat unsurprisingly, comes down to choice. The company points to cost, speed and portability, as well as the ability to use models fine-tuned on a developer’s own data. Users can choose between models running locally or through Ollama Cloud, and of course users are still able to lean on Anthropic’s frontier models wherever they like. Some developers also wondered how any of this differed from using Ollama with Claude Code, which was already possible. Claude Code is Anthropic’s terminal-based coding agent, and could already be pointed at Ollama’s Anthropic-compatible API to use local or cloud models. This release brings that same basic idea to the Claude Desktop app directly. “The future of AI is open models running everywhere work gets done.” For now, the new Claude Desktop integration is limited to Ollama’s Mac app, though Ollama suggested in replies on X that Windows support might be in the works . ‘Open models running everywhere work gets done’ Claude Desktop support arrives less than two months after Ollama raised a $65 million round of funding. In a statement issued at the time of the funding announcement in July, Ollama co-founder and CEO Jeffrey Morgan described a future in which open models are available wherever developers choose to work. “Open models should be easy to run, easy to build with, and available wherever people need them — on your own machine, in the cloud, or both,” Morgan said. “Ollama started as an open-source project, and has since grown into a community of millions of developers. Everything we do next is in service of that community and their best work. The future of AI is open models running everywhere work gets done — and Ollama is here to power this shift.” The update also builds on Ollama’s broader push to make local models easier to use across existing developer tools , while recent work such as native Apple MLX support has focused on improving local inference on Macs. Support for Claude Desktop is the latest expression of that strategy: let developers keep the apps they already use, while Ollama supplies the model underneath. The post Claude Desktop can now easily run Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi models — after Ollama’s first effort stalled appeared first on The New Stack .

items.title: I raised 5 kids and refused to spend thousands on youth sports. I don't regret it.
items.summary: The author had to say no to her kids when they wanted to play expensive sports. Courtesy of the author My son wanted to play hockey, but the cost and time commitment were too much for our family. My five kids tried several sports, but I kept our spending to a minimum. Now that they're adults, I'm glad I didn't chase expensive teams or potential scholarships. My oldest son tells a story about walking past the local sporting goods store every morning on his way to school and eyeing an ice hockey uniform he was eager to wear. The small town in Massachusetts where I raised my children was hockey central for the eastern region of the Commonwealth. Many of his friends first hit the ice at 3, learning to navigate the slippery surface by pushing plastic milk crates around the frozen field. Ice hockey was not in his future. It's an extremely expensive sport that requires a commitment from the whole family. With practices often scheduled for 5 a.m. and games as far away as Maine, there was no way I could support his dreams while also fulfilling his four siblings' dreams. I have no regrets for saying "no" to youth sports . We're big sports fans, but not great athletes Hockey was not the only game in town. Football, soccer, baseball, and basketball were all among the competitive sports offered to kids in our community. I signed the boys up for T-ball and the free Saturday morning instructional basketball program . I registered my daughter for gymnastics. All I wanted was for them to have fun with their friends and get a little exercise. Their interests ebbed and waned from season to season, but they enjoyed competing with and against their buddies. Only 1 of my sons showed real talent My third son is the only one of my boys to show any real athletic ability. At 10 years old, when he qualified to play A Division Little League , he was a top draft pick. His team won the championship that year, and it was a thrill to cheer them on to victory. When he found out there was an instructional, non-competitive hockey league in town, he asked to join. We borrowed a uniform and protective gear from his best friend, and trudged to the rink three afternoons a week from November to March. By mid-February, he was done. We were both tired of the long, grueling sessions in the freezing cold. We returned the equipment and never looked back, In middle school, he found lacrosse, which he defined as ice hockey on grass. He played on his school team through his senior year. Looking back, he regrets not playing baseball in high school. He thought he was probably better at baseball than lacrosse, but lacrosse attracted the girls. The players cultivated a hairstyle known as the flow , just a tuft of hair that peaked out of the back of their helmets, that seemed to be the main attraction for their groupies. Playing sports wasn't always their choice My two youngest children attended a startup school beginning in middle school. Because enrollment was low during those early years, every student was required to participate in at least one competitive sport on a no-cut team. My daughter chose soccer. My son, following in his brother's footsteps, picked lacrosse. Neither was a stand-out. I think I enjoyed the games more than they did because I could sit in the stands and chat with the other parents. That's why I missed the flagrant foul hit by an aggressive competitor that resulted in my son getting a concussion. It wasn't severe, but it did keep him in a dark room and out of school for a week. When he transferred schools for his senior year, he declined to play a sport. He'd already fulfilled that requirement for graduation and just didn't have the interest in spending time on a field any longer. In college, he toyed with the idea of playing intramural lacrosse, but other interests intervened, and he never picked up a stick again. I'm glad I only spent the minimum on sports for my kids. Today they prefer watching games from the sidelines or on TV a lot more than they ever did on the field. Read the original article on Business Insider

Their interests ebbed and waned from season to season, but they enjoyed competing with and against their buddies.

Only 1 of my sons showed real talent

My third son is the only one of my boys to show any real athletic ability. At 10 years old, when he qualified to play A Division Little League, he was a top draft pick. His team won the championship that year, and it was a thrill to cheer them on to victory.

When he found out there was an instructional, non-competitive hockey league in town, he asked to join. We borrowed a uniform and protective gear from his best friend, and trudged to the rink three afternoons a week from November to March. By mid-February, he was done. We were both tired of the long, grueling sessions in the freezing cold. We returned the equipment and never looked back,

In middle school, he found lacrosse, which he defined as ice hockey on grass. He played on his school team through his senior year.

Looking back, he regrets not playing baseball in high school. He thought he was probably better at baseball than lacrosse, but lacrosse attracted the girls. The players cultivated a hairstyle known as the flow, just a tuft of hair that peaked out of the back of their helmets, that seemed to be the main attraction for their groupies.

Playing sports wasn't always their choice

My two youngest children attended a startup school beginning in middle school. Because enrollment was low during those early years, every student was required to participate in at least one competitive sport on a no-cut team. My daughter chose soccer. My son, following in his brother's footsteps, picked lacrosse. Neither was a stand-out.

I think I enjoyed the games more than they did because I could sit in the stands and chat with the other parents. That's why I missed the flagrant foul hit by an aggressive competitor that resulted in my son getting a concussion. It wasn't severe, but it did keep him in a dark room and out of school for a week.

When he transferred schools for his senior year, he declined to play a sport. He'd already fulfilled that requirement for graduation and just didn't have the interest in spending time on a field any longer. In college, he toyed with the idea of playing intramural lacrosse, but other interests intervened, and he never picked up a stick again.

I'm glad I only spent the minimum on sports for my kids. Today they prefer watching games from the sidelines or on TV a lot more than they ever did on the field.

items.title: I got the chance to speak to Dolly Parton, and she was full of great life lessons. These are my favorites.
items.summary: Dolly Parton taught us so many life lessons. Paul Natkin/Getty Images Dolly Parton died on Tuesday. She was 80 years old. I had the chance to interview Parton, and she was full of great life lessons. Here are just a few of my favorites. When I was first invited to speak to Dolly Parton in 2022, I spent hours upon hours digging through her old interviews. I wanted to find new things to ask the woman who had already been famous for half a century . Today, I found myself doing the same thing. Not to prepare for an assignment, but to mourn the fact that I'll never get to chat with Parton, who died Tuesday at the age of 80, again. Parton was so many things — a songwriter, a performer, an actor, a fashion icon, a philanthropist, a cookbook author — yet she was so unquestionably singular. So unapologetically herself. She taught us many lessons. These are just a few of my favorites. "I don't like to be like everybody else." Harry Langdon/Getty Images As news of Parton's death reverberated around the world, one clip that quickly began circulating on social media was her 1978 interview with Barbara Walters . During their sit-down, the journalist told Parton, "You don't have to look like this. You're very beautiful. You don't have to wear the blonde wigs, the extreme clothes, right?" "It's certainly a choice," Parton replied. "I would never stoop so low as to be fashionable; that's the easiest thing in the world to do." That interview was nearly 50 years ago, and yet it feels more relevant than ever in a time when it seems the algorithm is making us all look, dress, and talk the same. Parton didn't care about trends. She loved sparkles, so she wore them. She loved big hair, so she teased it. And she loved her makeup so much, she wore it to bed . Parton told me she wasn't one to buy trendy or expensive products. She just used what worked best for her. "I don't think you have to pay a ton of money to have good products," she said. "Most of the products that cost less are just as good, and sometimes better, as the ones that cost a fortune. I don't buy for fame; I just buy the ones that work for me." There's no one-size-fits-all approach to productivity. Donaldson Collection/Getty Images One of my favorite fun facts to share with people is that Parton wrote "Jolene" and "I Will Always Love You" on the same night. Can you imagine? Most of us can barely make dinner after work , and here Parton is, writing two of the most important songs in America's discography within hours of each other! There was no big secret to her productivity, no fancy optimization hacks. Parton realized when she got her best work done and stuck to it — even if that meant waking up at 3 a.m. "I don't require as much sleep as a lot of other people do," she told me. "That's kind of a Parton family trait." I probably won't try to write my next article before dawn. But next time I feel creatively stuck, I'll take note of that fateful night when Parton's pen struck gold twice. "When I wrote those songs… I remember just sitting in the corner of this couch by this fireplace that was in the first house that Carl and I ever owned," she told me. "I just remember the den having so much atmosphere to write. There was something about that fireplace, the coziness, and that corner — the one corner of the couch where I was always sitting with my feet up, writing and singing my songs." Food can be a real love language. Dolly Parton and her husband, Carl Dean. dollyparton/Instagram Parton and her husband, Carl Dean, were married for nearly 59 years before Dean died in March 2025, yet there are almost no public pictures of them together. Dean didn't like the spotlight; Parton loved it. They never pressured each other to change. When the couple could spend time together at home, Parton was usually cooking up a storm. She once excitedly described to me all the things that she loved to make for Dean : French toast with bacon, biscuits and gravy, cornbread and pinto beans, fried chicken and coleslaw. "I just cook whatever comes to mind and whatever I'm in the mood for," she added. "I can cook any of it!" If they were going out to eat, Parton said she and Dean would get into "that little camper of ours" and make their way to a drive-thru ( Taco Bell was a favorite ). "Oh, I love to get a good burger out on the highway and french fries like everybody else," she said. "There's some really good fast-food restaurants. And we go get hot doughnuts now and then. It depends what we're in the mood for, whether it's tacos or burgers or whatever — we can go get it!" Shine a light on those who need it most. Dolly Parton and Dr. Carla Hayden, the Librarian of Congress, present the 100 millionth book to The Library of Congress on February 27, 2018 in Washington, DC. Shannon Finney/Getty Images My interviews with Parton mostly focused on food, and one recipe I had always wanted to ask her about — but always ran out of time — was her mother's stone soup. In her 1994 memoir, "Dolly: My Life and Other Unfinished Business," Parton revealed that her mother would always make stone soup for dinner if someone in the family was feeling down. Parton and her 11 siblings knew that if stone soup was on the menu, they had to go outside and pick a special pebble. The pebble that Parton's mom dropped inside the soup was always from the child who needed an extra few sips of love that day. "I can remember the feeling of having my stone picked to go in the soup," Parton wrote in her memoir. "There was magic in those stones and a lot of wisdom in that mother." As I read all the tributes that referenced Parton's lifetime of philanthropy — the Imagination Library, the LGBTQ+ advocacy, the medical research, the disaster relief — I kept thinking about that soup. When Parton found fame, she had all the pebbles in the world. It was her turn to make stone soup. Always be willing to laugh at yourself. Ron Davis/Getty Images Parton was always quick with a joke, even when it meant making fun of herself. One of my favorite moments from our interviews was when I asked if she had any fashion regrets . "Oh hell yeah, there's a bunch of them!" she exclaimed. "When I'm going through pictures for books or whatever, I literally laugh out loud and I think, 'Oh my Lord, you must have thought you looked good.' And I must have, or I wouldn't have worn it! But now it's like, 'Oh, Lord, have mercy.'" Parton was an icon, but she never took herself too seriously. I'm going to remember her words the next time I cringe at pictures of myself from 2012. Don't be afraid to age. Parton in a Dallas Cowboys cheerleader uniform at The Salvation Army's Red Kettle Kickoff Halftime Show on Thanksgiving Day in 2023. Ron Jenkins/Getty Images During our last interview together, I asked Parton to share her thoughts on aging in Hollywood, and she promptly responded: "Dollywood and Hollywood are two different places." "Of course, everyone would like to stay 35 forever, and in my mind, I kind of do," she added with a laugh. "But I can't get caught up in that trap of thinking I've got to do this or that. The way I live and the way I work, and the way I feel, I'm going to make every moment count." "I may live to be 100, or I may die tomorrow," she continued. "But whenever that is, I will know I died trying, and I will know I've done everything I could to make the most of everything that I could." Talk about words to live by. As I went through my interview notes, I saw all the questions I had compiled for Parton but never asked. Some were very silly — "What revenge dish would you make Jolene?" and "Please explain your crush on Jimmy Fallon" — others were more reflective. But they made me realize another life lesson. Ask all the questions you can, while you still have the chance. Read the original article on Business Insider

"I can remember the feeling of having my stone picked to go in the soup," Parton wrote in her memoir. "There was magic in those stones and a lot of wisdom in that mother."

As I read all the tributes that referenced Parton's lifetime of philanthropy — the Imagination Library, the LGBTQ+ advocacy, the medical research, the disaster relief — I kept thinking about that soup.

When Parton found fame, she had all the pebbles in the world. It was her turn to make stone soup.

Always be willing to laugh at yourself.

Ron Davis/Getty Images

Parton was always quick with a joke, even when it meant making fun of herself. One of my favorite moments from our interviews was when I asked if she had any fashion regrets.

"Oh hell yeah, there's a bunch of them!" she exclaimed. "When I'm going through pictures for books or whatever, I literally laugh out loud and I think, 'Oh my Lord, you must have thought you looked good.' And I must have, or I wouldn't have worn it! But now it's like, 'Oh, Lord, have mercy.'"

Parton was an icon, but she never took herself too seriously. I'm going to remember her words the next time I cringe at pictures of myself from 2012.

Don't be afraid to age.
Parton in a Dallas Cowboys cheerleader uniform at The Salvation Army's Red Kettle Kickoff Halftime Show on Thanksgiving Day in 2023.

Ron Jenkins/Getty Images

During our last interview together, I asked Parton to share her thoughts on aging in Hollywood, and she promptly responded: "Dollywood and Hollywood are two different places."

"Of course, everyone would like to stay 35 forever, and in my mind, I kind of do," she added with a laugh. "But I can't get caught up in that trap of thinking I've got to do this or that. The way I live and the way I work, and the way I feel, I'm going to make every moment count."

"I may live to be 100, or I may die tomorrow," she continued. "But whenever that is, I will know I died trying, and I will know I've done everything I could to make the most of everything that I could."

Talk about words to live by.

As I went through my interview notes, I saw all the questions I had compiled for Parton but never asked. Some were very silly — "What revenge dish would you make Jolene?" and "Please explain your crush on Jimmy Fallon" — others were more reflective. But they made me realize another life lesson.

Ask all the questions you can, while you still have the chance.

items.title: Your Coworkers Are Becoming “Meat Proxies” for AI
items.summary: Last year, netizens coined a new term to reflect our growing disdain for AI bots slowly usurping our human agency. The word “clanker” — later described as a “derogatory slur ” by Google’s AI Overview — set the stage for growing disillusionment and anger aimed at tech that’s cluttering our minds and feeds, while driving us crazy at work. And now we have the perfect accompanying pejorative to describe certain coworkers who are getting a little too carried away, blindly copy-pasting the output of AI chatbots — or slop, in today’s vernacular — without any form of revision or editing. That term is “meat proxies,” and we have a good feeling it’s going to catch on. The slang expression perfectly encompasses ongoing concerns over willingness to give over critical thinking skills to the machine, a phenomenon researchers have dubbed “ cognitive offloading ” or “ cognitive surrender .” It’s a particularly serious predicament for students, who are struggling to participate in class discussions , complete their homework , or even learn how to read long texts . Developer Niklas Gruhn, who’s widely credited for coining the term “meat proxy,” spoke to the frustration an increasing proportion of white collar workers are facing in a blog post earlier this month . He pleaded for people to stop regurgitating the “giant response” of a chatbot “verbatim.” “Please don’t do this,” he wrote. “I mean, I’ve done this. But I’ve been on the receiving end too many times now. This is not adding value.” “I can talk to Claude myself,” Gruhn added. “It’s going to be faster and I get to control the context. I don’t need a meat proxy in between.” Instead of brainlessly copying slop, the developer advised people to “read it, understand it, validate it, and then write a response in your own words.” “Making that effort is value you can add,” Gruhn argued. pic.twitter.com/MlqTL9zhnl — Abhi Aiyer (@abhiaiyer) August 23, 2026 The new term appears to hit a nerve, particularly among developers, who’ve seen the industry upended by the advent of powerful AI-powered coding software. “I already use that term for middle management,” one X user joked . “I think everyone knows at least one Meat proxy in their company,” another wrote . “This is the biggest career risk of 2026,” developer Cory House tweeted . “I’m seeing this problem first hand.” “There’s a very fine line between using AI to be more productive and being a meat proxy,” tech founder Nicholas Charriere added . “Don’t be a meat proxy.” Months before Gruhn coined the latest term, author and noted AI critic Cory Doctorow published a book about effectively the same phenomenon. In his “ Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI ,” Doctorow used the term “reverse centaur” to describe a metaphorical human being with a horse’s head — instead of the other way around — who mindlessly assists the machine. “In automation theory, a ‘centaur’ is a person who is assisted by a machine,” he wrote in the book. “You’re a human head being carried around on a tireless robot body. Driving a car makes you a centaur, and so does using autocomplete.” “And obviously, a reverse centaur is machine head on a human body, a person who is serving as a squishy meat appendage for an uncaring machine,” he added. But Doctorow didn’t rule out a more optimistic vision of the future where humans can regain control over their own agency. “There is one thing SF writers know that the AI bosses who are gunning for generational dynastic wealth by transforming us all into AI-lashed reverse centaurs do not know, and that they absolutely don’t want you to know,” he wrote. “That thing is this: the future is up for grabs. It is not inevitable. AI isn’t a genie that can’t be put back into a bottle.” More on cognitive offloading: Concern Grows That AI Is Damaging Users’ Cognitive Abilities The post Your Coworkers Are Becoming “Meat Proxies” for AI appeared first on Futurism .
items.summary_html:
Last year, netizens coined a new term to reflect our growing disdain for AI bots slowly usurping our human agency.

The word “clanker” — later described as a “derogatory slur” by Google’s AI Overview — set the stage for growing disillusionment and anger aimed at tech that’s cluttering our minds and feeds, while driving us crazy at work.

And now we have the perfect accompanying pejorative to describe certain coworkers who are getting a little too carried away, blindly copy-pasting the output of AI chatbots — or slop, in today’s vernacular — without any form of revision or editing.

That term is “meat proxies,” and we have a good feeling it’s going to catch on.

The slang expression perfectly encompasses ongoing concerns over willingness to give over critical thinking skills to the machine, a phenomenon researchers have dubbed “cognitive offloading” or “cognitive surrender.” It’s a particularly serious predicament for students, who are struggling to participate in class discussions, complete their homework, or even learn how to read long texts.

Developer Niklas Gruhn, who’s widely credited for coining the term “meat proxy,” spoke to the frustration an increasing proportion of white collar workers are facing in a blog post earlier this month. He pleaded for people to stop regurgitating the “giant response” of a chatbot “verbatim.”

“Please don’t do this,” he wrote. “I mean, I’ve done this. But I’ve been on the receiving end too many times now. This is not adding value.”

“I can talk to Claude myself,” Gruhn added. “It’s going to be faster and I get to control the context. I don’t need a meat proxy in between.”

Instead of brainlessly copying slop, the developer advised people to “read it, understand it, validate it, and then write a response in your own words.”

“Making that effort is value you can add,” Gruhn argued.

pic.twitter.com/MlqTL9zhnl

— Abhi Aiyer (@abhiaiyer) August 23, 2026

The new term appears to hit a nerve, particularly among developers, who’ve seen the industry upended by the advent of powerful AI-powered coding software.

“I already use that term for middle management,” one X user joked.

“I think everyone knows at least one Meat proxy in their company,” another wrote.

“This is the biggest career risk of 2026,” developer Cory House tweeted. “I’m seeing this problem first hand.”

“There’s a very fine line between using AI to be more productive and being a meat proxy,” tech founder Nicholas Charriere added. “Don’t be a meat proxy.”

Months before Gruhn coined the latest term, author and noted AI critic Cory Doctorow published a book about effectively the same phenomenon. In his “Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI,” Doctorow used the term “reverse centaur” to describe a metaphorical human being with a horse’s head — instead of the other way around — who mindlessly assists the machine.

“In automation theory, a ‘centaur’ is a person who is assisted by a machine,” he wrote in the book. “You’re a human head being carried around on a tireless robot body. Driving a car makes you a centaur, and so does using autocomplete.”

“And obviously, a reverse centaur is machine head on a human body, a person who is serving as a squishy meat appendage for an uncaring machine,” he added.

But Doctorow didn’t rule out a more optimistic vision of the future where humans can regain control over their own agency.

“There is one thing SF writers know that the AI bosses who are gunning for generational dynastic wealth by transforming us all into AI-lashed reverse centaurs do not know, and that they absolutely don’t want you to know,” he wrote. “That thing is this: the future is up for grabs. It is not inevitable. AI isn’t a genie that can’t be put back into a bottle.”

More on cognitive offloading: Concern Grows That AI Is Damaging Users’ Cognitive Abilities
